title: All Saints (1 November)

lines: ONE FEAST FOR ALL OF THEM.
cards: The Church's calendar is crowded with saints: apostles and martyrs, popes and peasants, page after page of names, each with a day. Yet behind those names, the Church believes, there's a crowd beyond counting.
A farmer in a village nobody's heard of who prayed every morning of his life. A night nurse. A man who quietly forgave his brother.
No statue, no day, no feast. So once a year the Church throws them all one party.

teach.b: The feast grew from the martyrs. In the early centuries there were so many that no calendar could hold them, and Christians in the East began keeping one day for all martyrs together.
In Rome, Pope Boniface IV took the Pantheon, the old temple to all the Roman gods, and dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs.
Later, Pope Gregory III dedicated a chapel at Saint Peter's to all the saints, and the first of November became the date, spreading across the West.

teach.h: A MULTITUDE NO ONE COULD NUMBER.
teach.b: The reading comes from Revelation, in the Douay-Rheims: "After this I saw a great multitude, which no man could number, of all nations, and tribes, and peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne."
Which no man could number. That's the point. In Catholic teaching, a saint isn't only someone the Church has formally canonized.
Canonization says, with confidence, this person is in heaven and can be held up as an example.

But everyone in heaven is a saint, and the Church assumes that's a huge crowd, most of them never named. The Gospel is the Beatitudes: blessed are the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the peacemakers.

teach.h: A GREAT MULTITUDE, WHICH NO MAN COULD NUMBER.
teach.b: Not a list of well-known deeds; a description of ordinary people living a certain way. All Saints is a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation. And it opens a two-day pair: tomorrow, all who have died.

how: Catholics celebrate All Saints on 1 November as a solemnity and, in many countries, a holy day of obligation, with the Beatitudes as the Gospel; in some parishes children dress as saints the evening before.

games.q: you're choosing the Gospel for a feast of all the saints, well-known and unknown. which fits?
o: the Beatitudes: the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful.
the calling of the twelve apostles.
games.why: the Church reads the Beatitudes: not a list of well-known deeds, but a description of ordinary people living a certain way.

practice: Let someone come to mind whose goodness nobody ever wrote down: a relative, a teacher, the woman who ran the parish soup kitchen, a neighbor who checked on everyone, living or dead. Picture their hands and what those hands did.
If you pray, thank God for them, or ask their prayers, as Catholics do; if you don't, simply honor them in silence.

wordCard.voice: All Saints. The first of November, a feast for every saint in heaven, the known and the unknown, the multitude no one could number. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: holy, set apart — the root of the word saint.

carryVoice: Your line: the ones nobody knew. Most saints, Catholics believe, were never named. See you tomorrow.
